previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old female with a history of coronary artery disease, mitral regurgitation, and prior kidney and pancreas transplants was admitted with worsening chest pain, shortness of breath, and cough. She had recently been treated for a presumed pneumonia, but imaging and clinical course revealed her symptoms were due to an exacerbation of systolic heart failure with pulmonary edema rather than infection. Her chest pain was attributed to demand ischemia from increased cardiac strain. An echocardiogram showed worsened mitral regurgitation and reduced heart function. She was treated with IV nitroglycerin, diuresis, and transitioned to oral heart failure medications. Her kidney function declined temporarily, with creatinine peaking at 5.1, but improved to 3.4 by discharge without requiring dialysis. She received two units of packed red blood cells for symptomatic anemia, and Bactrim was discontinued due to drug-induced pancytopenia. She was discharged home on optimized medical therapy with close follow-up planned with cardiology and nephrology.
